principles.text: Back founders on ambition, speed at unblocking themselves and technical depth; the idea itself matters little.
Build something you genuinely care about, or you'll quit the first time it gets really hard.
Start by solving your own problem; Curse began as an add-on database for his WoW guild.
Make the core service free and reach the whole addressable audience before worrying about monetization.
Paying customers are the best funding; a $500K pre-seed is plenty for most lean software teams.

sampleQA.question: What do you look for before writing a pre-seed check?

answer.text: He mostly invests on vibe: ambition, how fast you find ways to unblock yourself, and how technical you are. He asks about the idea only to gauge your ambition.
Green flags: started building before pitching investors, obsessively talks to users, finds creative marketing channels, and won't give up.
You should be able to explain the product in one sentence, clearly, with no buzzwords.
With Curse Voice, monetization was not his worry; the goal was getting all of the roughly 100M hardcore PC gamers outside China onto the platform first.
Curse ran two revenue channels: advertising for the free audience and a subscription for premium features.
Ads were added when costs outgrew what he could cover himself.

sampleQA.question: How should I market an early product?

answer.text: Build cool things, tell people about it, then keep telling more people. Repeat forever.
Skip stealth mode: if no one knows you exist, you don't exist. Build loud.
Move fast on channels: test several growth channels in a day and make many videos with different hooks. Use AI as an editor, not a ghostwriter.
